introduction: Bahá’u’lláh begins with a correction: God is “exalted beyond and above proximity and remoteness,” and “that some are near and others are far” belongs to us. The guide follows the consequences through letters and prayers. Nearness is of the soul and not of place; many who stand close are far, and many far away are near; separation in God’s path can be union; remoteness is the real fire; and the smallest turning is met more than half way. The psalms have always prayed this way, asking not to be cast away from the presence and why God stands afar off. The Qur’án speaks of a God nearer than the jugular vein, and the two sayings of the Prophet that ‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes are given here in full. Jesus’s parables of the publican and the prodigal, Augustine’s “thou wert with me, but I was not with thee,” Pascal, Donne and Marlowe’s exiled spirit belong to the same country. A few voices ask harder questions: the psalmist who feels forsaken without cause, the gulf that is fixed, Socrates on examining oneself, and Hopkins, for whom the world is not a distance from God.
questions: Bahá’u’lláh says God’s relationship to His creatures “knoweth no degrees”; the nearness and farness are ours. How does that change the way you read the psalmist’s “why standest thou afar off?”
“How many who are near are far and know it not.” Jesus says the same of priests and publicans. What kinds of outward nearness are most likely to hide inward distance today?

Several readings say that separation “was the essence of nearness.” Dickinson says parting is “all we know of heaven, and all we need of hell.” When has distance from someone brought you closer, and when has it simply been loss?

The Báb knows “no fire more intense than remoteness,” and Marlowe’s spirit says “this is hell, nor am I out of it.” What does it mean to locate heaven and hell in nearness and distance and not in places?
“One must not look at one’s self,” says ‘Abdu’l-Bahá; Socrates insists on the examined life. How can both be honoured?
“Whoso draweth nigh unto Me a span, I draw nigh unto him a cubit,” and the prodigal’s father runs. What small turnings do the last readings have in mind, and what makes them hard?

outside.why: God is “exalted beyond and above proximity and remoteness.” Isaiah holds both ends: the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity dwells in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit.

“That some are near and others are far is to be ascribed to the manifestations themselves.” Jeremiah hears the question put by God: am I a God at hand, and not a God afar off? Do not I fill heaven and earth?

“How many near ones are strangers, and how many strangers are near!” Told that his mother and brethren stand outside, Jesus points to his disciples: whosoever shall do the will of my Father, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother.
Kinship is not what makes for nearness. Proverbs: there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
“Nearness is verily of the soul, not of the body.” Jesus’s figure for it is the branch and the vine: abide in me, and I in you.
“That which looks outwardly near is in fact distant.” Isaiah: this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me.

Absence and presence depend on “the purity of the receiving place”; a polished surface shows the sun. Paul: we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image.

The spirit never withdraws; only the mirror clouds. The twenty-second psalm speaks as one from whom God has withdrawn, and who has done nothing to cloud the glass: why art thou so far from helping me? Does the reading’s account cover his case?
“This nearness dependeth upon clearness, purity.” The beatitude: blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.
The old saying that “the Friend is nearer to me than myself” is called strange, and then deepened. Augustine’s version of it: thou wert with me, but I was not with thee.
“In that very remoteness lieth nearness.” Pascal hears it said to him in his night of prayer: console thyself, thou wouldst not seek Me, if thou hadst not found Me.
A nearness “that hath no likeness” in the realm of places. The psalmist, after envying the prosperous, ends here: it is good for me to draw near to God.

A rank that “despite its perfect nearness is remote, and despite its perfect remoteness is near.” The Ísha Upaniṣad of the Self: it is far, and likewise near; it is inside all this, and it is outside all this.
“Though thou art far from the seat of the Throne, yet thou art near.” Ephesians to its Gentile readers: ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh.
“How many who are near are far and know it not.” Jacob, waking at Bethel: surely the Lord is in this place; and I knew it not.
Those who were near “were deprived of what they desired.” Jesus in the synagogue of his own town: no prophet is accepted in his own country.
The far stand before His face. Jesus to the chief priests in the temple: the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you.
“How many who were near were kept back, and how many who were remote attained!” Luke: they shall come from the east and west; there are last which shall be first, and first which shall be last.

“The one who dwelt in the desert attained … while he who was in the mosque remained deprived.” In Jesus’s parable the Pharisee prays in the temple, and the publican, standing afar off, goes home justified.
“If thou art absent in body, thou art present in heart and spirit.” Paul to a church he had never seen: though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit.
“Thou art mentioned in this assembly and art present in this meeting.” Paul to Thessalonica: being taken from you for a short time in presence, not in heart.
“Thou art near, not far; present and in attendance.” The last words of Matthew’s Gospel: lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes Sa‘dí: no wall stands between lover and beloved. Donne, leaving on a journey: our two souls endure not yet a breach, but an expansion, like gold to airy thinness beat.
“A nearness … which no remoteness can affect.” Paul: neither death, nor life, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God.

“That very separation was the essence of nearness.” Emily Dickinson allows parting half of that: parting is all we know of heaven, and all we need of hell. Is the reading’s paradox a consolation, or a discovery?
“This parting is endless reunion.” Jesus to his disciples on the night of parting: ye now therefore have sorrow, but I will see you again, and your joy no man taketh from you.
“The substance of the grief is the essence of the visit.” Rúmí’s reed is cut from the reed-bed, and its whole song comes of the cutting.
“Dispersion is unity and wandering is freedom.” Acts on the first persecution: they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.

For the friends, being strangers to one another is “mercy and bounty.” Gibran gives distance a place even between those who are together: let there be spaces in your togetherness. What does distance give that closeness cannot?
Material separation and union “have absolutely no effect.” Shakespeare: love is not love which alters when it alteration finds, or bends with the remover to remove.
“In the extremity of remoteness, may [you] attain the utmost degree of nearness.” At Sinai the people stood afar off, and Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was.
“A nearness after which no remoteness followeth.” David’s prayer after his fall: cast me not away from thy presence.
“The time of remoteness hath passed.” The Song of Solomon: for, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone.
“The most manifest of the manifest and the most hidden of the hidden!” Augustine’s address to God piles up the same opposites: most hidden and most near.
“Whose nearness is my desire, Whose presence is my dearest wish.” The psalmist: whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.
“Whose court is my goal.” One thing have I desired of the Lord: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.

“Burn me with the fire of Thy dominion, then prescribe for me to meet Thee.” Rábi‘a of Basra prayed that if she worshipped for fear of hell she might burn in it, and that the everlasting Beauty be not withheld from her.
Loneliness and sighing “in this wilderness” for the sight of the Presence. David in the wilderness of Judah: my soul thirsteth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, to see thy power and thy glory.
“If Thou didst destine for me remoteness from that most holy garden.” Jonah, from the deep: I am cast out of thy sight; yet I will look again toward thy holy temple.
“Put a stop to this consuming separation.” The psalm: how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?
“Suffer me … to draw nigh unto Thee.” Francis Thompson tells the story from the side of one who fled, down the nights and down the days, and was pursued. Who closes the distance in these prayers?
“Others yearn for it from afar.” Job: behold, I go forward, but he is not there; and backward, but I cannot perceive him.
Hearts “consumed in their remoteness and separation.” As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.
“Suffer me not … to be far removed from the shores of nearness.” The psalmist’s shortest form of the prayer: be not far from me; for trouble is near.
“Distance me not, O my Beloved.” A psalm asks it as a question: why standest thou afar off, O Lord? why hidest thou thyself in times of trouble?
“Deprive not Thy servants from drawing nigh unto the seat of Thy Cause.” Hebrews: let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace.

“Save them from the chasm of separation.” In Jesus’s parable Abraham tells the rich man that the chasm cannot now be crossed: between us and you there is a great gulf fixed. Do these prayers assume that no separation is final?
A prayer for what will “draw them nearer.” Moses says the means are already close: the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it.
“God is nearer to you than your own selves.” The Qur’án’s verse: We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.
“Will ye not see?” The Qur’án, of those who stand round a deathbed: We are nearer unto him than ye are, but ye see not.
Nearness to God is by drawing nigh to Him Whom God shall make manifest. Jesus makes the same claim for himself: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.

The Báb ties nearness to recognition of a person. Paul tells the philosophers of Athens that God is not far from every one of us, for in him we live, and move, and have our being. How do the general nearness and the particular one fit together?
“Leave them not to themselves for less than the twinkling of an eye.” Moses’s blessing: the eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms.

Yearning hearts drawn to the horizon “above which the Day-Star of Thy beauty sheddeth its radiance.” Malachi: unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings.
The lost one guided, the thirsty quenched, the dead brought to life. The father of the prodigal: this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.
“We have heard your call.” The Qur’án: when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh; I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto Me.
“The Glance of Divine Providence has ever been turned towards that direction.” The Qur’án: He is with you wheresoever ye may be.
“Thou art … mentioned in the Most Holy Court.” Malachi: a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the Lord, and that thought upon his name.
Verses recited to draw the hearer near. The Prophet is told to say of his Lord: lo! He is Hearer, Nigh.
One believer is mentioned by name from the Most Luminous Horizon. The Qur’án on being known wherever one is: there is no secret conference of three but He is their fourth.
“Blessed art thou for having … drawn nigh unto God.” A psalm: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
“Thou hast walked with thy feet towards God and turned with thy spirit.” A pilgrim psalm: blessed is the man in whose heart are the ways of them.
Some said the monastery, others the mosque; he rests nowhere but in the divine sanctuary. Kabír’s God answers the seeker: I am neither in temple nor in mosque; I am beside thee.
“This bewildered, passionate one finds rest nowhere” else. Augustine: our heart is restless, until it repose in thee.
“The heart findeth no rest save through the Day-Star of assurance.” The psalmist to himself: return unto thy rest, O my soul.
“Take shelter beneath the protection of God’s Beauty.” The psalm of refuge: he shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust.

“If you seek an impregnable fortress, seek the shadow of the Glorious Lord.” He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty: my refuge and my fortress.
“If thou desirest to find solace in anyone, find it in My Self.” Isaiah: as one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you.
Drawn “from the west of remoteness to the east of nearness,” into holy company. Jesus: many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob.
To “migrate from the abodes of limitations to the treasuries of eternity.” Hebrews on Abraham: he went out, not knowing whither he went, for he looked for a city which hath foundations.
A call from “the branch of Fire” to ascend to the retreats of nearness. The voice from the bush says how to come near: draw not nigh hither; put off thy shoes.
“Far better to spread our wings and fly from this perilous depth.” The psalmist: oh that I had wings like a dove! for then would I fly away, and be at rest.
“That station is nearness at the Threshold of God.” The last vision of the Bible: his servants shall serve him, and they shall see his face.

“I know of no fire more intense than remoteness from Thee.” Marlowe’s Mephistopheles, asked how he comes to be out of hell: why, this is hell, nor am I out of it, having seen the face of God and lost it.
Remoteness as the fire. Paul’s phrase for final loss names no flames: destruction from the presence of the Lord.
“To be veiled from Him is still more grievous than all these torments.” The Qur’án’s judgment on the heedless is put in the same terms: on that day they will be veiled from their Lord.
Hell is “the state of mind” in which a person is separated from God. Milton’s Satan, looking at Eden: which way I fly is Hell; myself am Hell.
Good thoughts and deeds “bring men nearer to God, and that is heaven.” Jesus: the kingdom of God cometh not with observation; the kingdom of God is within you.

“One must not look at one’s self,” for that way lie guilt and uselessness. Socrates held that the unexamined life is not worth living. Is there a self-examination that does not end in looking at oneself?

Looking at ourselves “we see only our weakness.” Adam, having seen his nakedness, hides among the trees, and the first question in the Bible is God’s: where art thou? Who creates the distance in that story?
“The nearer you are to God, the further you are from the world.” Hopkins found God by looking harder at the world: the world is charged with the grandeur of God. Which “world” does the reading mean?
He commanded what draws near and forbade what makes remote. Moses: I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing; therefore choose life.
“We summon you at all times unto God.” Isaiah: seek ye the Lord while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near.
Called “from estrangement in transient, passing homelands” to eternal abodes. Hebrews: they confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth, and desire a better country.
A prayer that the veils be rent, so that nearness is attained. Matthew, at the death of Jesus: the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom.
Let them not “deprive their eyes … nor prevent their ears.” Jesus on why he speaks in parables: they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not.
“Whoever turned attained … whoever remained heedless was deprived.” The invited guests of the parable: they all with one consent began to make excuse.
Let not the heedlessness of others keep thee from the direction of the All-Merciful. The psalmist: I have set the Lord always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.
So firm that all the peoples of the earth could not remove them from “the ocean of nearness.” Ruth to Naomi: intreat me not to leave thee; whither thou goest, I will go.
“Hold fast unto the cord of My loving-kindness.” Jesus: I am the vine, ye are the branches; without me ye can do nothing.
“Abasement is exaltation itself.” Mary’s song: he hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.
To “daily progress” toward acceptance. Proverbs: the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day.
“Thy desire is to attain nearness to the divine Threshold.” The psalmist: my soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the Lord.
“I love children exceedingly, for they are near unto the Kingdom of God.” Jesus: suffer little children to come unto me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven.
Nearness is where we begin. Wordsworth on the child: trailing clouds of glory do we come from God, who is our home; heaven lies about us in our infancy.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá addresses someone as the dawning-place of this saying. Here it is as al-Bukhárí records it: My slave keeps on coming closer to Me through voluntary devotions till I love him.
Drawing nigh through devotion. The Qur’án’s earliest chapter ends with the same pairing: prostrate thyself, and draw near.
The tradition ‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes, as al-Bukhárí gives it, goes on: if he comes to Me walking, I go to him running.
“The slightest turning of man toward God becomes the cause of infinite nearness.” The Letter of James: draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you.
A span answered by a cubit. In Jesus’s parable the son sets out for home, and when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and ran.

hadith-span-and-cubit.text: if he comes one span nearer to Me, I go one cubit nearer to him; and if he comes one cubit nearer to Me, I go a distance of two outstretched arms nearer to him; and if he comes to Me walking, I go to him running
hadith-span-and-cubit.author: Muḥammad
hadith-span-and-cubit.caveat: A saying in which the Prophet reports God’s words (ḥadíth qudsí).

hadith-nearer-through-voluntary-works.text: My slave keeps on coming closer to Me through performing Nawafil (praying or doing extra deeds besides what is obligatory) till I love him, so I become his sense of hearing with which he hears, and his sense of sight with which he sees
hadith-nearer-through-voluntary-works.author: Muḥammad

rights.note: Modern translation (translator d. 2021); part of one sentence.

hadith-nearer-through-voluntary-works.caveat: A saying in which the Prophet reports God’s words (ḥadíth qudsí).

psalm-good-to-draw-near.text: But it is good for me to draw near to God: I have put my trust in the Lord God, that I may declare all thy works

psalm-be-not-far-from-me.text: Be not far from me; for trouble is near; for there is none to help

psalm-cast-me-not-away.text: Cast me not away from thy presence; and take not thy holy spirit from me

isaiah-far-off-and-near.text: I create the fruit of the lips; Peace, peace to him that is far off, and to him that is near, saith the Lord; and I will heal him

deuteronomy-god-so-nigh.text: For what nation is there so great, who hath God so nigh unto them, as the Lord our God is in all things that we call upon him for

ephesians-far-off-made-nigh.text: But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ

matthew-publicans-go-before-you.text: Verily I say unto you, That the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you

mark-not-far-from-the-kingdom.text: And when Jesus saw that he answered discreetly, he said unto him, Thou art not far from the kingdom of God

exodus-thick-darkness-where-god-was.text: And the people stood afar off, and Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was

genesis-where-art-thou.text: And they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the Lord God amongst the trees of the garden. And the Lord God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou

jonah-cast-out-of-thy-sight.text: Then I said, I am cast out of thy sight; yet I will look again toward thy holy temple

thessalonians-from-the-presence-of-the-l.text: Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power

proverbs-closer-than-a-brother.text: A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother

john-abide-in-me.text: Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me

luke-last-which-shall-be-first.text: And they shall come from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south, and shall sit down in the kingdom of God. And, behold, there are last which shall be first, and there are first which shall be last

quran-veiled-from-their-lord.text: Nay, but surely on that day they will be covered from (the mercy of) their Lord.

quran-prostrate-and-draw-near.text: Nay, Obey not thou him. But prostrate thyself, and draw near (unto Allah).

quran-hearer-nigh.text: Say: If I err, I err only to my own loss, and if I am rightly guided it is because of that which my Lord hath revealed unto me. Lo! He is Hearer, Nigh.

marlowe-why-this-is-hell.text: Why this is Hell, nor am I out of it. / Thinkst thou that I, that saw the face of God, / And tasted the eternall joyes of Heaven, / Am not tormented with ten thousand Hels, / In being depriv'd of everlasting blisse
marlowe-why-this-is-hell.author: Christopher Marlowe
marlowe-why-this-is-hell.caveat: The spelling is that of the early editions.

quran-nearer-than-ye-are.text: And We are nearer unto him than ye are, but ye see not

jeremiah-god-at-hand.text: Am I a God at hand, saith the Lord, and not a God afar off? Can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? saith the Lord. Do not I fill heaven and earth

pascal-wouldst-not-seek-me.text: Console thyself, thou wouldst not seek Me, if thou hadst not found Me
pascal-wouldst-not-seek-me.author: Blaise Pascal
